phase1.explanation:
A class can live inside another class, and Java gives you four flavors depending on how tightly coupled you want it.

A plain [[term:inner class]] — `class InnerClass` written directly inside `OuterClass`, no `static` — [[key:has full access to the outer object's fields, even private ones]], but that access comes at a cost: you need an actual outer instance to create one, written as `outer.new InnerClass()`.

A [[term:static nested class]] drops that requirement — [[key:no outer instance needed, but it also loses access to the outer object's instance members]], since there's no specific outer object it's tied to. Create one with `new Outer.StaticNestedClass()`.

A [[term:local inner class]] is defined right inside a method body, and [[key:it only exists and is only usable within that one method]] — useful for a helper that genuinely has no reason to exist anywhere else.

And an [[term:anonymous inner class]] skips naming entirely — you write the whole class body inline, on the spot, usually to implement an interface or extend a class for exactly one use, like the `Runnable` in the example.

[[key:Picking between them comes down to coupling]]: use a regular inner class when it's genuinely tied to a specific outer instance, static nested when it isn't, and anonymous for quick one-off implementations you'll never reuse.

phase2.errorMessage:
Outer.java:7: error: non-static variable message cannot be referenced from a static context
            System.out.println(message);  // ERROR!
                               ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:A static nested class has no connection to any specific Outer instance]] — that's the whole point of marking it static. So when `Inner` tries to read `message`, an instance variable that only exists once an Outer object has actually been created, there's genuinely no outer object for it to read from.

[[key:There are three honest fixes here]]: make `message` static too, if it should be shared across all Outer instances regardless of which one you're looking at; make `Inner` a regular (non-static) inner class instead, which DOES keep a connection to a specific outer instance; or pass an actual Outer instance in and read `outer.message` explicitly. [[key:Static nested classes are really just top-level classes that happen to be packaged inside another class for organization]] — they don't get any special access to instance state just by being nested.

mcq.question:
What can a non-static (regular) inner class access that a static nested class cannot?

A) Static methods of the outer class
B) The outer class's instance fields and methods, even private ones
C) Nothing — they have identical access
D) Other classes in the same package

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a class Library with:
• Private field: name (String)
• Inner class: Book with fields title, author
• Method in Library: addBook(String title, String author) that creates a Book
• Method: listBooks() that prints all books

In main, create a Library, add 2 books, and list them.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: before lambda expressions arrived in Java 8, anonymous inner classes — like the Runnable example you just saw — were THE standard way to write a quick one-off implementation of an interface, especially for GUI event listeners. Lambdas can now replace many of those cases with far less boilerplate, but anonymous inner classes are still exactly what a lambda compiles down to under the hood for interfaces with a single method.
